articles.title: ISRO Successfully Launches India's First Imaging Satellite For Geosynchronous Orbit
articles.content: Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp SRIHARIKOTA, Sep 4: ISRO on Friday successfully launched EOS-05, India’s first Earth observation satellite intended for a geosynchronous orbit, aboard the GSLV-F17 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre here, marking a significant milestone for the country’s space programme. The state-of-the-art spacecraft, weighing 2,367 kg, is designed to provide real-time imagery and support applications including agriculture and disaster management. The satellite was launched towards the Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO) in the pre-dawn hours. The three-stage GSLV-F17 lifted off at 2.55 AM from the second launch pad after a smooth 27-hour countdown that began at 11.30 PM on Wednesday. Despite the early hour and rain, a large number of members of the public gathered at the spaceport to witness and cheer the launch. Unlike several Earth observation satellites operating from low Earth orbit (LEO), EOS-05 is intended to operate at an altitude of about 36,000 km above Earth in geosynchronous orbit. At this altitude, the satellite will match the rotational speed of Earth, enabling continuous observation of the region. The GSLV-F17 is the 19th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle . The 51.7-metre rocket has a cryogenic third stage and a lift-off mass of 420.5 tonnes, with the satellite housed inside the rocket’s nose cone. The mission is also significant as it follows the unsuccessful GSLV-F10/EOS-03 mission in 2021. That mission was aborted 307 seconds after launch, with an investigation pointing to an anomaly in the Cryogenic Upper Stage. Friday’s launch came after a gap of nearly eight months following the failure of ISRO’s PSLV -C62 mission on January 12, when the rocket carrying 16 satellites failed to place them into the intended orbit due to an anomaly in its third stage. An earlier PSLV-C61/EOS-09 mission in May 2025 had also failed following a motor pressure issue and a fall in chamber pressure. (Agencies)

articles.title: ISRO Launches EOS-05, India's First Imaging Satellite From Geosynchronous Orbit | Science & Tech
articles.content: Bhubaneswar: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on Friday successfully launched EOS-05, India’s first imaging satellite designed to operate from a geosynchronous orbit, aboard the GSLV-F17 from Sriharikota, marking a significant milestone in the country’s Earth observation capabilities. The 51.7-metre-tall, 420.5-tonne three-stage rocket lifted off from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at 2.55 am and successfully placed the approximately 2,367-kg Earth observation satellite into its intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit. The mission marked the 19th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) and the 107th launch from Sriharikota. ISRO chairman Dr V Narayanan said the satellite was injected into the intended orbit precisely, underlining the improved performance of the launch vehicle. Speaking from the Mission Control Complex after the launch, Narayanan said the GSLV had come a long way since its first flight, when it carried a payload of 1,536 kg. “With EOS-05, the vehicle has carried the heaviest payload in its history at 2,367 kg. We gradually improved the performance of the vehicle by optimising the structural mass and improving the propulsion system,” he said. He added that EOS-05 was India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from a geosynchronous orbit and would provide strategic data. EOS-05 was injected into a geosynchronous transfer orbit with a nominal perigee of 171 km, an apogee of 31,026 km and an inclination of 19.28 degrees. The satellite will subsequently be moved to its final orbit through a series of orbital manoeuvres using onboard thrusters. The GSLV-F17 carried an S139 solid core with four L40H liquid strap-ons, a GL40HT liquid second stage and a CUS15 indigenous cryogenic upper stage. The rocket was also equipped with a four-metre composite ogive payload fairing. The successful launch is also significant for the GSLV programme, which is designed to place heavier payloads into geosynchronous and geostationary orbits. Friday’s mission was ISRO’s second orbital mission of 2026 and the first GSLV mission since GSLV-F16 successfully placed the joint NASA-ISRO NISAR Earth observation satellite into a 743-km sun-synchronous orbit on July 30, 2025. The first orbital mission of 2026, PSLV-C62 carrying EOS-N1 and other payloads, had failed following an anomaly towards the end of the rocket’s third-stage flight on January 12. Following the successful launch, ISRO posted pictures of the lift-off on X and declared the mission a success. “Mission Success! GSLV-F17 has successfully accomplished its mission, placing EOS-05 into the intended orbit,” the space agency said. Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated ISRO and described the mission as “yet another outstanding achievement” and a proud moment for the nation. “The successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, India’s first-ever imaging satellite from geosynchronous orbit, is a reflection of the excellence, innovation and growing capabilities that define India’s space sector,” Modi said in a post on X. He also highlighted the growing partnership between ISRO and Indian industry, saying it was adding new strength and scale to India’s space programme and expanding capabilities across the space ecosystem. articles.title: ISRO's 'Naughty Boy' rocket makes a strong comeback, boosting India's space ambitions
articles.content: News Report ISRO’s ‘Naughty Boy’ rocket launched, boosting India’s space ambitions By The Pamphlet September 4, 2026 Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp India’s space programme received a major boost on Friday, September 4, as the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched the GSLV-F17 carrying the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite. Nicknamed the “Naughty Boy”, the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) has earned a reputation over the years for its unpredictable record. Its latest success, therefore, carries significance far beyond a routine satellite launch. The GSLV-F17 mission is particularly important because EOS-05 is designed to operate from a geosynchronous orbit, around 36,000 kilometres above Earth. It is India’s first dedicated imaging satellite intended for this type of orbit and is expected to provide continuous observation of the country and surrounding regions. Such a capability can have applications ranging from disaster management and infrastructure monitoring to strategic and national-security surveillance. The success also comes at a crucial moment for ISRO. The agency has faced recent setbacks involving the PSLV, traditionally regarded as its workhorse launch vehicle. The PSLV-C62 mission encountered an anomaly in January 2026, leading to a detailed investigation. Against this backdrop, the successful GSLV-F17 mission demonstrates that India retains multiple indigenous launch capabilities rather than depending on a single rocket family. The “Naughty Boy” nickname itself reflects the GSLV’s complicated history. The rocket has experienced failures during its development and operational journey, making every successful flight an important demonstration of engineering maturity. Yet its story is also one of perseverance. Developing the cryogenic propulsion technology needed for more demanding missions was a major technological challenge for India. Mastering this technology strengthened the country’s ability to independently launch heavier satellites into higher orbits. That self-reliance is perhaps the biggest significance of the GSLV-F17 mission. Space technology is closely connected to national capability, communications, Earth observation, navigation, scientific research and strategic security. Having indigenous launch vehicles reduces dependence on foreign providers and gives India greater control over when and how important satellites are placed in orbit. The mission also fits into a much larger transformation of India’s space programme. In recent years, ISRO has achieved milestones including Chandrayaan-3’s historic lunar landing, the Aditya-L1 solar mission and the SPADEX demonstration of autonomous docking and undocking. India has also operationalised several indigenous launch vehicles, including PSLV, GSLV, LVM3 and SSLV. The GSLV-F17 success therefore represents more than the revival of one rocket. It reinforces India’s growing ability to build, launch and operate increasingly sophisticated space systems independently. For a country preparing for human spaceflight through Gaganyaan, developing a national space station and expanding its commercial space sector, reliable launch capability is indispensable. Every successful mission adds experience, confidence and technological know-how. The “Naughty Boy” may have lived up to its mischievous nickname in the past, but its latest performance sends a different message, the message being that India’s space programme is becoming more resilient, more self-reliant, and increasingly capable of taking on ambitious missions of its own. articles.title: Jaishankar defends Russian oil trade, says 'buying or not buying oil' won't end Ukraine war
articles.content: Jaishankar defends Russian oil trade, says 'buying or not buying oil' won’t end Ukraine war By - MPost Update: 2026-09-04 05:00 GMT Kyiv: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has defended India’s continued purchase of Russian crude oil, saying that stopping or continuing such purchases would not bring an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. Speaking in Kyiv after meeting Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, Jaishankar said the five-year-old conflict could only be resolved through dialogue, diplomacy and negotiation, rather than decisions over the purchase of oil, minerals, metals or fertilisers. Responding to questions over India’s Russian oil imports, Jaishankar highlighted the challenge of meeting the energy needs of 1.4 billion people at a time when global energy conditions remain difficult. He said India respects Ukraine’s position on the issue but expects other countries to respect India’s perspective as well. His remarks came amid Western pressure on countries continuing to buy Russian energy. The US Senate last month passed a bipartisan bill that could allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries, including India and China, that continue importing Russian oil and gas. Russia has remained India’s largest crude oil supplier despite the pressure. India imports around 88% of its crude oil requirements from overseas, with roughly one-third coming from Russia. Indian purchases of Russian crude rose sharply after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, when Western countries reduced their purchases from Moscow. However, imports declined in August after reaching record levels in June and July. India imported around 2.1 million barrels of Russian crude per day in August, accounting for more than 40% of its total crude imports. Russia has also become increasingly dependent on Asian buyers such as India and China after European sanctions restricted its access to Western markets. Steady demand from Indian refiners has helped Russian exporters maintain shipments despite restrictions affecting shipping, insurance and financial services.

Features Science ISRO’s ‘Naughty Boy’ performs better than expected; what it means for the EOS-05 satellite After an 8-month nap, ISRO drops India’s first-ever continuous imaging satellite into orbit, and it’s already flexing extra fuel. Soumya Pillai 04 September, 2026 10:47 am IST Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin ISRO's 'Naughty Boy' EOS-05 satellite launches into orbit | X/@isro Follow Us : Text Size: A- A+ New Delhi: The Indian Space Research Organisation successfully launched the GSLV-F17 rocket from Sriharikota early on 4 September, placing the much-awaited EOS-05 earth observation satellite into its intended orbit. The GSLV rocket, often referred to as the “Naughty Boy” because of its initial string of failures, rose to the occasion and performed better than expected in its third stage, injecting the satellite into a geosynchronous transfer orbit with a nominal perigee of 171 kms, an apogee of 31026 kms and an inclination of 19.28 degrees. Perigee and apogee are the closest and furthest points in an object’s elliptical orbit around the Earth. According to ISRO’s mission document, EOS-05 was to be initially placed in an orbit of 171 km x 28934 km, after which the satellite would perform its orbit-raising manoeuvre to an altitude of 36,000 km. Show Full Article The EOS-05 satellite is India’s first-ever imaging satellite designed to operate from a geosynchronous orbit. Unlike other low Earth orbit satellites that pass over a set location periodically, the EOS-05 satellite is designed to maintain a continuous monitoring of Indian territory and the surrounding regions from a vantage point nearly 36,000 km above Earth. It would ensure a closer and consistent observation of the Indian territory and go a long way in providing critical information about weather systems, disasters, infrastructure monitoring and the general surveillance of the region. What does this mean for EOS-05? The GSLV-F17 rocket gave EOS-05 more orbital energy than planned. Its highest point above Earth is about 2,092 kms higher than the expected target. This is good news for the satellite because the spacecraft now has less work to do with its own propulsion system to reach its eventual geosynchronous operating orbit. To attain its final geosynchronous altitude of about 36,000 kms above the equator, EOS-05 will use its onboard propulsion to raise its orbit from a sub-GTO and circularise it at that altitude. Senior ISRO officials, on the condition of anonymity, told ThePrint that since the satellite has saved some of its onboard propellant, it can be used later, potentially increasing the satellite’s operational life. “The mission life of an earth observation satellite is anywhere between five to seven years. articles.title: "Significant stride in India's space journey": Rajnath Singh after GSLV-F17 launch
articles.content: New Delhi [India], September 4 (ANI): Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Friday hailed the successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, terming it another significant stride in India's space journey and highlighting the satellite's contribution to the country's Earth-observation capabilities. In a post on X, the Defence Minister wrote, "The successful GSLV-F17 launch carrying EOS-05 marks another significant stride in India’s space journey. As India’s first imaging satellite placed in Geosynchronous orbit, EOS-05 strengthens our Earth-observation capabilities and reflects the growing sophistication of our space programme." The GSLV-F17 vehicle successfully and precisely injected EOS-05, also known as the geo-imaging star satellite, into its intended orbit, marking another milestone for India's space programme, Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) Chief V Narayanan announced on Thursday. Singh also highlighted the expanding partnership between the ISRO and the country's industrial sector, saying that collaboration was contributing to innovation and strengthening indigenous capabilities. He added, "Under the visionary leadership of PM Shri @narendramodi, India is steadily building a progressive, self-reliant and globally competitive space ecosystem. The expanding partnership between ISRO and Indian industry is giving greater scale to innovation, strengthening indigenous capabilities and opening new frontiers for our space ambitions." Earlier in the day, ISRO chief V Narayanan announced that the GSLV-F17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the Advanced Earth Observation Satellite-05 (EOS-05), the geo-imaging star satellite, into its intended and required orbit. Narayanan said the successful mission was a significant achievement for India’s space programme and that the satellite’s health was perfectly alright after its injection into orbit. “I am very happy to announce that the GSLV-F17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the Advanced Earth Observation Satellite 05, the geo-imaging satellite, in the intended and required orbit,” Narayanan said right after the mission success was announced at the space center. He added that once EOS-05 is operationalised in orbit, it will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo orbit and provide important strategic data for the country. “Today, we have injected the heaviest satellite, 2367 kgs, using this launch vehicle. The health of the satellite is perfectly alright,” the ISRO chief said. Narayanan credited the successful mission to the collective efforts of the entire ISRO team, along with its industrial partners and the academic community. “This success is the culmination of the hard work of the entire ISRO team along with our industrial partners and academia. On this occasion, I congratulate each and every one of you. This is a great achievement in our country’s space programme,” he said. ISRO successfully deployed the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite into orbit from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota on Friday, marking another major milestone in India’s space programme. The launch took place from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, SHAR. The launch was carried out on a GSLV-F17 rocket, which is the 19th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV), as it carried EOS-05 towards a Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO). (ANI)

articles.content: EOS-05 separating from GSLV-F17 rocket's final stag The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) today (4 September) successfully launched EOS-05, the country's first Earth observation satellite designed to operate in geosynchronous orbit, marking a significant milestone in India's space programme. The 2,367-kg satellite was placed in the intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit approximately 18 minutes after lifting off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. The GSLV-F17 rocket, standing 51.7 metres tall with a lift-off mass of 420.5 tonnes, carried what is now the heaviest satellite ever launched by a GSLV vehicle. Unlike conventional Earth observation satellites that operate from low Earth orbit, EOS-05 will hover at an altitude of roughly 36,000 km above Earth, matching the planet's rotational speed to maintain a fixed position over the Indian subcontinent. Also known as GISAT-1A, the satellite is designed to provide near real-time Earth imagery for applications including agriculture monitoring, disaster management, environmental assessment and strategic surveillance. Today's launch marked ISRO's first successful mission of 2026, following a gap of nearly eight months. The achievement serves as a replacement for the unsuccessful GSLV-F10/EOS-03 mission of August 2021, when an anomaly in the cryogenic upper stage led to mission failure. With this success, India joins an elite group of nations operating geostationary Earth imaging satellites, strengthening the country's remote sensing capabilities from one of the highest operational altitudes for civilian Earth observation platforms. articles.content: SRIHARIKOTA: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on Friday successfully launched its GSLV-F17 rocket carrying the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite , marking the space agency’s second successful rocket launch of the year. The 2,367-kg satellite was injected into its designated sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (sub-GTO) shortly after the rocket lifted off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota at 2.55 am. The launch came despite heavy rain in the Sriharikota region at the time of liftoff. With all the rocket’s systems, telemetry and control parameters found to be normal and the automated launch sequence functioning as expected, the mission director Thomas Kurian gave the final clearance for the launch at the scheduled time. The GSLV-F17 mission is particularly significant as EOS-05 is intended to restore the Earth observation capability lost with the failure of the GSLV-F10 mission in August 2021. The earlier mission carried EOS-01, also known as GISAT-1, but the satellite was lost after the cryogenic upper stage of the launch vehicle failed to ignite. The first and second stages of GSLV-F10 had performed normally after liftoff. However, a technical anomaly in the cryogenic upper stage had resulted in the failure of the third stage engine to ignite, eventually leading to the loss of EOS-03. Nearly five years later, ISRO has successfully placed EOS-05 in orbit, paving the way for the restoration of continuous Earth observation capabilities. EOS-05 is a civilian and strategic Earth observation satellite designed to provide frequent and near real time imagery of large areas of the country. It is equipped to capture images in multispectral and hyperspectral bands under cloud free conditions. According to the mission objectives, the satellite is expected to provide images of selected regions at frequent intervals, with observations of some areas possible every five minutes. It is also designed to cover the entire Indian landmass at intervals of around 30 minutes, with a spatial resolution of approximately 42 metres. The data generated by the satellite is expected to support a wide range of applications, including weather monitoring, disaster management, agriculture, forestry and surveillance. Its capabilities will be useful for monitoring floods, cyclones, forest fires and other natural disasters, besides supporting strategic and national security requirements. articles.content: BENGALURU: The GSLV-F17 (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle) carrying EOS-05 executed a textbook launch at 2.55 am on Friday. After setbacks during previous missions, Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) teams worked continuously to ensure the mission's success, with the GSLV-F17 placing the EOS-05 satellite into a Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit at 3.14 am. Friday's launch marked the space agency's maiden success for the year 2026. The EOS-05 is India’s first ever imaging satellite to monitor from Geosynchronous orbit about 36,000 km above the Earth. ISRO teams noted that this is the heaviest satellite ever launched into a geosynchronous orbit, with a lift-off mass of 420.5 tonnes. The 51.7-metre-tall vehicle was launched from the second launch pad of the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota amid light rain. A beaming ISRO chief V Narayanan said, "I am very happy to announce that the GSLV F-17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the advanced EOS-05 geo imaging satellite in the intended and required orbit." "This is the 107th launch from Srihariharikota and the 19th mission of GSLV," he said soon after the launch. Narayanan added that this was the second launch of the financial year and the first for ISRO. Six more launches have been targeted for this financial year, including NVS-03. The teams are also working on the Gaganyaan mission, with the first uncrewed mission under the programme scheduled for launch during this financial year, he said. Former ISRO directors Dr K Radhakrishnan, K Kiran Kumar and S Somanath were also present at the launch site, along with teams from the Indian Air Force and the Indian Navy. The GSLV-F17 launch comprised three stages, solid, liquid propulsion and cryogenic. Loud cheers erupted in the launch room when the successful completion of the cryogenic stage was announced by the directors 15 minutes after the launch, overcoming the earlier hiccups faced during the cryogenic stages of previous missions. The GSLV-F17 has an S139 solid core and four L40H liquid strap-ons. The normal perigee is 172 km and apogee is 29,000 km, but ISRO achieved a 171-km perigee and an apogee of 31,260 km, Narayanan announced on the occasion. The inclination of the satellite is 19.28 degrees, while the payload mass is 2,367 kg, making it the heaviest satellite launched by India so far, he said. articles.title: Nepal floods: India offers DNA tests for immediate relatives of missing people - Firstpost
articles.content: As Nepal struggles to identify hundreds of disaster victims, India has opened its forensic network to families of missing persons India has opened its network of government forensic laboratories to help families identify relatives who went missing in the devastating natural disasters in Nepal. Under the initiative, first-degree biological relatives of missing people can provide DNA samples at designated forensic facilities across India. The samples will be used to help identify unidentified bodies recovered in Nepal. The initiative has been launched by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs in coordination with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), following flash floods and ice-rock avalanches in Nepal that killed more than 1,200 people and left thousands unaccounted for. Parents, children and siblings of missing persons living in India can provide biological samples for DNA profiling. The move is aimed at speeding up the identification process and helping families get clarity about the fate of their loved ones. Under the new arrangement, eligible relatives can visit designated government forensic facilities to have their samples collected and analysed. The testing will use Autosomal STR (Short Tandem Repeat) DNA profiling, a method widely used in disaster victim identification. The facilities involved include Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs), State Forensic Science Laboratories (SFSLs), laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) in Gandhinagar and its regional campuses, as well as NABL-accredited public forensic institutions. Once the DNA profiles are generated, they will be shared with authorities and disaster victim identification teams in Nepal. The profiles can then be compared with DNA obtained from unidentified remains recovered from the disaster-hit areas. Automated DNA database systems can be used to help identify possible matches. India has also sent a 19-member Disaster Victim Identification (DVI) team to Nepal to support the identification effort on the ground. The team includes forensic scientists and DNA experts from the NFSU and CFSL Delhi. They will work with teams at the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory in Kathmandu. The experts will assist with collecting and analysing forensic evidence and matching DNA profiles of missing people with unidentified remains. Identifying victims after large-scale floods, landslides and other natural disasters can be extremely difficult. Bodies may be severely damaged or decomposed, making visual identification unreliable or impossible. In such situations, DNA profiling can provide a more reliable way of establishing a victim’s identity. DNA matches can eventually provide families with confirmation and help authorities ensure that victims are formally identified.

articles.title: Sriharikota: ISRO Roars Back into Action - Deccan Chronicle
articles.content: Sriharikota: In a spectacular early-morning display of technical brilliance, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) Sriharikota at 2:55 AM on Friday. Leaving a trail of orange flames that pierced the darkness, the 51.7-metre-tall GSLV lifted off majestically from the Second Launch Pad and zoomed into the night sky with textbook precision. The flawless execution sparked immediate celebration, bringing immense delight to scientists at the Mission Control Room and the crowds gathered at the visitors gallery, unmindful of the downpour, to witness the historic event. Weighing 420.5 tonnes at lift-off, the three-stage Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV)—equipped with an indigenous cryogenic upper stage and a 4-metre-diameter ogive composite payload fairing—perfectly deployed the Earth Observation Satellite-05 (EOS-05) into its targeted Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO). Operating from an altitude of around 36,000 km, EOS-05 marks a monumental milestone as India’s first-ever imaging satellite stationed in a geosynchronous orbit. The state-of-the-art spacecraft is engineered to provide advanced, real-time Earth observation data, vastly strengthening the country's capabilities in land monitoring, environmental tracking, and disaster management. Notably, EOS-05 serves as a highly anticipated replacement for the GISAT-1A satellite, which was lost during a launch failure in 2021. The high-stakes mission was closely watched worldwide, carrying immense weight for India's space program. Following an uncharacteristic seven-month pause triggered by anomalies in two successive PSLV missions—including the PSLV-C62 mission on January 12—ISRO had temporarily halted launches to conduct exhaustive technical reviews. The flawless performance of GSLV-F17 effectively breaks the hiatus, completely restoring momentum and reinforcing global confidence in ISRO’s launch vehicles. With this triumph, ISRO not only puts an end to its brief dry spell but firmly establishes a sophisticated new sentinel in space, marking another giant leap in India's expanding interplanetary and Earth-observation footprint.

articles.content: Updated 4 September 2026 at 03:52 IST ISRO successfully launches EOS-05 aboard GSLV-F17, giving India a new eye in the sky and a major boost after recent launch setbacks. Shruti Sneha Science News 5 min read Follow : ‘Naughty Boy’ Delivers: ISRO Successfully Launches GSLV-F17 Carrying EOS-05, India’s New ‘Eye In The Sky’ | Image: Republic New Delhi: The wait ended at 2:55 am on Friday as the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05 from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, marking a major step forward for India's Earth observation capabilities. The launch comes at an especially crucial time for ISRO. Following a series of setbacks with its Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), which was formerly regarded as one of the world's most reliable rockets, the agency has entered a challenging phase. With the PSLV now grounded while investigations and tests are underway, the success of GSLV-F17 might provide a significant boost to confidence in India's space program. September 3, 2026 However, the two launchers belong to separate families and have different propulsion systems. The PSLV's recent issues are thus not directly related to the GSLV Mk II, allowing Friday's mission to be evaluated on its own technical merits. Why this GSLV mission is being watched closely The GSLV has a complex history. Inside ISRO, it is popularly known as the "naughty boy" because to its inconsistent performance during its development years. Six of the first 18 flights did not complete their missions successfully. However, the same rocket has played a significant part in India's efforts to develop the ability to launch larger satellites. At the heart of this voyage is the indigenous cryogenic engine. During the 1990s, India requested cryogenic technology from Russia, but the US strongly opposed the transfer due to fears about missile proliferation. International regulations eventually stopped India from obtaining the technology it desired. ISRO subsequently tackled the significantly more difficult challenge of developing the technology domestically. Indian scientists had to perfect cryogenic propulsion systems that used liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen at temperatures below minus 250 degrees Celsius. After years of development, testing, failures, and redesigns, India was finally able to create its own cryogenic upper stage. That achievement marked a significant milestone in India's launch program and remains one of the defining technologies of the GSLV Mk II. The rocket's capabilities have also been internationally validated. The GSLV Mk II was tasked with launching NISAR, the world's most costly civilian Earth imaging satellite, demonstrating confidence in the launcher's ability to perform hard missions. Friday's trip will be the nineteenth flight. EOS-05: An eye that can keep watching India The satellite riding aboard GSLV-F17 is critical to the mission's success. EOS-05, also known as GISAT-1A, weighs about 2,367 kg and is intended to operate from geosynchronous orbit, roughly 36,000 kilometers above Earth.
